newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Ifo says EMU doubts could kill German upturn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ifo says EMU doubts could kill German upturn.

text.p: Germany's accelerating recovery could be killed off if doubts about the stability of the planned European single currency force the Bundesbank to raise interest rates, a leading research institute said on Tuesday.

The Munich-based Ifo institute said in its economic outlook that weakness in the mark had caused an export boom which meant economic growth would speed up to 2.25 percent in 1997 and 2.75 percent in 1998, while inflation would stay modest.

It urged the government to seize on the present "optimum" environment to implement vital reforms of the tax system and labour market or risk missing a unique chance to overcome the rigidities that have kept unemployment stubbornly high.

The institute said it had based its growth forecast on the assumption that the mark will not weaken further, with the dollar remaining between 1.80 marks and 1.90 marks through 1998 and the Bundesbank raising rates only slightly in the period.

But it warned that if the mark and other European currencies continued to fall on fears the euro will be soft, European central banks may have to tighten policy significantly to shield their economies from imported inflation.

An alternative scenario, although less likely, was that expectations of a delay of the euro's launch, scheduled for January 1, 1999, could cause the mark to surge and choke off the export boom that has been driving the economy, Ifo said.

Willi Leibfritz, an economist at Ifo, said he could imagine a dollar strengthening above 1.90 marks "could set alarm bells ringing" at the Bundesbank and prompt it to take "small steps" to send a signal to financial markets.

Leibfritz's comments contributed to pushing the dollar up to above 1.88 marks, a fresh eight-year high, amid continung market speculation that the Bundesbank may raise its main money market rate, the repo rate, to stem the mark's slide.
The central bank kept markets guessing on Tuesday by calling for bids for securities repurchase funds at an unchanged fixed rate of three percent.
Financial markets had speculated that the central bank could offer a second set of funds under different conditions.

A decision to set a second securities repurchase pact at variable interest rates -- where banks bid for funds at the interest rates of their choosing -- would have been a signal that the bank was prepared to let interest rates drift higher.
Speculation of such a move persisted in markets on Tuesday, although economists said the risks that any policy change could misfire, and even boost the dollar, were now also growing.

"Seen overall, the conditions for a continuation of the economic upturn are good but there are substantial risks, particularly in connection with the planned European monetary union," Ifo said in the half-yearly report.
Ifo said rising exports had boosted capacity production in German industry to levels last seen in boom phases at the start of the 1970s and late 80s/early 90s.

The present constellation of a weak mark, low inflation, low interest rates and global trade growth presented Germany with "optimum conditions" to curb structural unemployment with tax cuts and labour market reform, Leibfritz said.

The phenomenon of a "split economy" with a booming export sector and stagnating domestic investment and private consumption will disappear only gradually but export growth should spill over into domestic demand in 1998, Ifo said.

That would help reduce unemployment to 4.26 million people or 11.1 percent of the workforce in 1998 from an estimated 4.3 million people or 11.3 percent in 1997. Last year unemployment averaged just below four million or 10.3 percent.
Employment would grow by 100,000 next year after shrinking by 500,000 in the past 12 months, but the gain was just a drop in the ocean given the extent of joblessness, Leibfritz said.

"If the necessary reforms are not tackled now but shelved until after the (October 1998) election, we will lose valuable time, fail to send a positive signal and run the risk of having to reform at a time when conditions are less favourable."
The Bonn government has vowed to press ahead with its tax reform plans which envisage 30 billion marks ($16 billion) in tax cuts, even if it takes until the turn of the century.
The reform has been blocked by the opposition Social Democrats who hold a majority in the upper house of parliament.
Consumer inflation should stay weak, averaging 1.75 percent in 1997 and rising to two percent in 1998, Ifo said.

Ifo also raised its forecast for Germany's deficit to 3.3 percent of gross domestic product from 3.2 percent in its last forecast. But it said that even a deficit of this level would not bar Germany from entering European monetary union.
